title: THE LAKE THAT OUT-HOLDS THE GREAT LAKES
subject: geography

contradiction.viewer_thinks: the Great Lakes hold the world's most fresh water
contradiction.actually: one single Siberian lake holds more than all of them combined

beats.narration: Ask where Earth keeps its fresh water, and most people picture the Great Lakes. The real answer is one lake in Siberia.
beats.claim: Lake Baikal alone holds more unfrozen fresh surface water than the North American Great Lakes combined
beats.visual_question: where is most of Earth's liquid fresh water?
beats.visual_answer: a single long lake in frozen Siberia, its depth not yet revealed

beats.narration: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth — and its water would cover all of North America about a metre deep.
beats.claim: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth; its volume spread over North America would cover it by roughly a metre
beats.visual_question: just how deep is one lake allowed to be?
beats.visual_answer: a cross-section sounding line dropping far past any other lake's depth

beats.narration: One thousand six hundred and forty-two metres deep, holding roughly one fifth of all the unfrozen fresh surface water on the planet.
beats.claim: Baikal holds roughly one fifth of Earth's unfrozen fresh surface water, at 1,642 metres the deepest lake
beats.visual_question: how much water does one rift valley gather?
beats.visual_answer: volume bars: one Baikal bar towering over the combined Great Lakes bar

beats.narration: The depth has an engine: Baikal sits in a rift, a tear in the crust that is still being pulled apart — so the basin keeps sinking.
beats.claim: Baikal lies in an active continental rift that keeps widening, so the basin keeps deepening
beats.visual_question: why is the lake still so deep?
beats.visual_answer: a crust cross-section being pulled apart, with the lake basin sinking between the shoulders

beats.narration: It is also the oldest lake on Earth. Some twenty-five million years of isolation built species that live nowhere else.
beats.claim: at roughly 25 million years Baikal is the world's oldest lake, and most of its species are endemics found nowhere else
beats.visual_question: what does twenty-five million years of isolation build?
beats.visual_answer: an ark of strange endemic species: transparent fish, sponge gardens on the deep floor

beats.narration: Then the impossibility: a seal, living and breeding a thousand kilometres from any ocean — and its route in is still argued about.
beats.claim: the Baikal seal (nerpa) lives and breeds entirely in fresh water, far from any ocean; its route there is debated
beats.visual_question: what is a seal doing a thousand kilometres from the sea?
beats.visual_answer: a seal resting on lake ice, the nearest ocean far beyond the horizon

beats.narration: Baikal is not a pond that got lucky. It is a living archive: ancient, deepening, still opening.
beats.claim: Baikal is an ancient, still-active rift lake that keeps deepening as the rift opens
beats.visual_question: so what is Lake Baikal, really?
beats.visual_answer: a living archive: a rift valley filling with twenty-five million years of water
